lead.topic: Striking EEB paper: ecological context and evolution of courtship neural circuits
lead.headline: Food smells switch on a fly's mating drive
lead.deck: A fruit specialist ties courtship to food odor and social motion through neural circuits that also exist in less dependent relatives.
lead.authors: Brand P, Keller K, Coleman RT, Eghbali NB, Zylka S, Prieto-Godino LL, Ruta V
paragraphs: Sexual selection is often described as a choice between individuals. In the fruit fly Drosophila erecta, the setting changes whether males court at all. Philipp Brand and colleagues studied this relative of D. melanogaster, which breeds seasonally on Pandanus fruit. In behavioral arenas, food-associated odors attracted flies to a patch and were required for sustained male pursuit of females. The researchers separated attraction to food from the drive to court: odor helped sustain arousal even when a prospective mate was available. By encouraging flies to move and inspect potential mates, the food patch also changed each male's visual scene.

That movement fed back on behavior. Visual motion generated by nearby flies further amplified arousal, creating a loop among smell, sight and group courtship. In related species, food odor could enhance arousal but was not required for vigorous courtship in D. melanogaster. Neural recordings and genetic manipulations identified broadly conserved courtship circuits whose responses to environmental signals differed between species. Evolution may therefore alter the thresholds of shared neural machinery rather than invent new mating circuits. The work provides a mechanism for concentrating reproduction around a temporary resource. It does not demonstrate that the seasonal availability of Pandanus fruit directly caused the stricter odor requirement to evolve.
lead.push: Test how males respond to natural Pandanus fruit odors across the fruiting season, rather than relying mainly on experimental food cues. Map genetic differences affecting sensory thresholds in crosses where possible. Does stronger odor dependence actually increase mating success on short-lived food patches, or does it simply prevent reproduction when those odors are absent?

people.name: Philipp Brand
people.bio: Philipp Brand leads the Evolutionary Neuroscience and Behavior group at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Frankfurt, a role he began in 2025. He earned his population biology PhD at UC Davis with Santiago Ramírez, then worked with Vanessa Ruta at Rockefeller. He studies how ecology changes sensory circuits and mating behavior.

people.name: Vanessa Ruta
people.bio: Vanessa Ruta is a professor at Rockefeller University, directs its Laboratory of Neurophysiology and Behavior, and is an HHMI investigator. She earned her PhD at Rockefeller with Rod MacKinnon and trained with Richard Axel at Columbia. Her laboratory investigates how neural circuits produce innate and learned behaviors and evolve across fly species.

slot2.headline: Gene pairs expose weak points in tuberculosis
slot2.cite: Kresse IJ et al. Nature (published 4 Nov 2026). Original paper.
slot2.body: Genes rarely act alone, but measuring their joint effects is difficult when essential genes cannot simply be deleted. Researchers built a dual CRISPR interference system that partly suppresses pairs of genes in mycobacteria and tracks their effects on growth. Across a model species and Mycobacterium tuberculosis, they screened more than four million guide-RNA combinations and identified over 15,000 genetic interactions, cases where the combined effects depart from predictions based on single genes. Interaction profiles linked poorly understood genes to cell functions and suggested drug-target combinations. Four synergistic compound pairs were validated in laboratory tests. This is a map for developing combinations, not a new tuberculosis treatment.

slot3.headline: Gas above Mars hints at sleeping volcanoes
slot3.cite: Trokhimovskiy A, Mège D et al. Science Advances (published 4 Nov 2026). Original paper.
slot3.body: An orbiter has found recurring spikes of hydrogen chloride above fissures on the flanks of Alba Mons, a giant Martian volcano. The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter measured the gas in early northern summer, when Mars normally has little atmospheric hydrogen chloride. Researchers compared the signal with surface geology and atmospheric chemistry and argue that gas escaping from buried magma could explain the pattern. Seasonal thawing might open paths through ice-blocked cracks. But no eruption or fresh lava flow has been observed, and a volcanic explanation remains an inference. If confirmed, subsurface heat could change where future missions look for water and potentially habitable environments.
